newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bankers convinced EMU on track, downplay gold plan.
newsitem.headline: Bankers convinced EMU on track, downplay gold plan.

text.p: Top bankers assembled for the International Monetary Conference (IMC) are still convinced that Europe's single currency, the euro, will start on schedule and are not overly worried about the furore sparked by Bonn's plans to revalue German gold reserves.

"There is a large consensus (among bankers) that we should be taking January 1, 1999 very seriously and not only because it is fixed in the Maastricht Treaty," Juergen Sarrazin, chief executive of Dresdner Bank AG told a briefing.
Sarrazin was speaking after a closed-door session with some 130 commercial bankers on the implication for financial services on Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Although clearly startled by the strong showing by the French Socialists in Sunday's election, many bankers noted that the French Socialists were essentially in favour of further European integration.
Hilmar Kopper, former chief executive of Deutsche Bank AG and now its supervisory board chairman, also said he was unfazed by Bonn's controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves.
Koppper said the timing of the revaluation plan might require more discussion but the project was not in itself a concern.
"I take a relaxed view on this," Kopper said. "One might argue over the timetable. But this is more a media issue than a real issue," he added.

The Bundesbank has rejected a plan put forward by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue central bank gold and currency reserves to market prices, arguing that it damaged central bank independence and undermined the credibility of Germany's efforts to meet the criteria for European econimic and monetary union (EMU).

Earlier German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had addressed the bankers and defended his controversial plan to revalue the gold reserves, saying the plan was not an attack on the vaunted independence of the Bundesbank.
"Let me state here, clearly and categorically: in no way does the revaluation of the Bundesbank reserves amount to an infringement of the independence of the Bundesbank," Kohl said.
"We know from decades of positive German experience that an independent central bank is a prime asset," he added.
Sarrazin made it clear that bankers took Kohl's reassurance seriously.
"Kohl made it clear how to look at the topic," he added.
Sarrazin said it was clear that other countries had also revalued their gold reserves and dismissed the notion that Bonn's plan amounted to "playing around with gold."

European Monetary Institute (EMI) president Alexandre Lamfalussy also said he did not see the pressure put on the Bundesbank by Bonn to revalue gold as undermining prospects for a fully independent European central bank.
Asked if he saw a risk to the independence of the European Central Bank from the project, Lamfalussy said:
"Not at all. I see no risk whatsoever to the independence of the European central bank."
The EMI is the forerunner to Europe's future central bank.
Asked about the impact of the election victory of the Socialists in France on Sunday, Sarrazin said the socialists had "made it quite clear that they were pro-European and pro-euro."
With the socialist election victory, Sarrazin said France would send new negotiators to Amsterdam for the talks on Maastricht II and then the impact of the change in government would become clear.
